content.p: On the night of Sunday 29 July 1990, soldiers of Liberia's national army entered the compound of St. Peter's Lutheran Church in Monrovia and killed a large part of the roughly 2,000 civilians who had taken shelter there. Survivors, human rights lawyers and a US federal court put the number of dead at about 600. The compound was a refuge set up under the Red Cross and the Liberian Council of Churches. Most of those inside were Gio and Mano people, members of groups that President Samuel Doe's soldiers suspected of backing the rebellion against him.

It is regarded as one of the worst single attacks on civilians in the First Liberian Civil War. For more than three decades afterwards, nobody in Liberia was tried for it. The ruling on who was responsible came from a civil court in Philadelphia, which in 2021 held a former army commander, Moses Thomas, liable for the attack. Thomas denies involvement and has never faced criminal charges.
content.h2: A city closing in on its president
content.p: By the summer of 1990 the seven-month-old civil war had reached the capital. The Los Angeles Times, reporting from Monrovia the day after the killings, described a three-cornered fight between Doe's forces and two rebel groups, one led by Prince Johnson and the other by Charles Taylor. Rebels controlled most of the city, and Doe was guarded by a few hundred soldiers at his seafront mansion.

The Center for Justice and Accountability, a legal group that later represented survivors, says the army became more aggressive towards civilians as the rebels gained ground, singling out Mano and Gio people whom it believed were loyal to Taylor. The Red Cross and the Liberian Council of Churches opened shelters in churches and other buildings, which together housed nearly 9,000 displaced people, according to the group. The New Dawn reported that the army had already attacked a United Nations compound and other places holding displaced people. By late July, as many as 2,000 people were sleeping in the church, its courtyard and the school building at St. Peter's. A legal writer at Just Security says Red Cross flags marked all four corners of the compound.

The Philadelphia Inquirer, summarising what the US court heard, says Doe believed the Mano and Gio population of Monrovia was more loyal to the rebels than to him. Thomas's unit, hoping to root out spies and rebels, was sent to pull people from their homes, detain them, or kill them in the streets. Families fled to shelters such as St. Peter's. According to the lawsuit, Thomas visited the compound in the days before the massacre and promised the people inside his protection.

Survivors told reporters in 1990 that about 30 government soldiers burst into the church on Sunday evening. Witnesses quoted by the Los Angeles Times said the troops broke the door down with machine-gun fire, then shot refugees at point-blank range and went up to the floor above to fire on hundreds more who were asleep. Some women who tried to leave with their children were ordered to one side and then fired on. One man who hid in the church attic said the refugees thought the soldiers had come to question them: "Then they started killing, and everyone began screaming and trying to hide."

The accounts given later to the US court describe the same shooting. Survivors said men, women and children were shot as they tried to flee, and that soldiers moved through the compound with machetes and bayonets to finish off anyone still alive. One survivor, a child at the time, hid near the pulpit; he was shot in the leg and was separated from his mother and brother for two years afterwards. Another plaintiff, who was sleeping in the courtyard, was bayoneted in the arm while lying among the bodies. A fourth said she waited hours after the soldiers left before she dared climb out, "soaked in others' blood". One plaintiff recalled hearing a soldier say that "not one Nimba man will leave".

Two former army members who testified in the case, and one of the plaintiffs, said they saw Thomas standing outside the gates directing the soldiers who opened fire. Witnesses said in sworn statements that he ended the attack after an hour with the words: "Everyone is dead. All soldiers out." According to the Inquirer, the court found that he had ordered 45 soldiers to kill everyone in the building.
content.h2: What reporters found, and what governments said
content.p: The Los Angeles Times reporter described a church floor thick with blood and bodies lying under the pews and on the altar. An injured woman lay on the steps pleading for her son; a man with a slashed neck called for water. A person who visited the church said some of the dead, apparently killed as they tried to escape, hung from the window frames. Since the church had no telephone, those inside could not call for help.

Doe's government blamed rebel guerrillas wearing government uniforms. The United States did not accept that. A statement from the Bush administration called the killings a "senseless act of terror" and blamed forces controlled by Doe, and a deputy press secretary, Hart, said US indications were that government troops were involved. The newspaper reported that Washington had no plans to send troops to Liberia to stabilise the situation, and quoted State Department spokesman Richard Boucher saying the United States did not see its role as intervening directly in the conflict.

The death toll was disputed from the start. Witnesses told the newspaper at least 600 had been killed, while State Department officials, working from reports by embassy staff still in Monrovia, put the figure closer to 200. Later legal and journalistic accounts settled on about 600 or "more than 600". The Inquirer says the bodies were left to rot until volunteers buried them two months later.

The killing did not end at the church gates. According to a Liberian survivors' account carried by The New Dawn, some of the wounded were killed at John F. Kennedy Hospital and other medical sites where they sought treatment, and others were taken to the north end of the airport runway, near a mangrove swamp, and murdered.
content.h2: Thirty years without a trial in Liberia
content.p: Liberia's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2009 and identified the church massacre as one of the key atrocities of the civil wars. According to The New Dawn, it recommended that Doe, who was dead by then, and other former soldiers be prosecuted. Just Security reports that the commission also recommended an Extraordinary Criminal Tribunal for wartime crimes, and that Liberia has done little to carry out its recommendations on prosecutions, reparations and memorials. The same article says that some commentators blame a lack of political will, and that others, including former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, have worried that pursuing prosecutions would endanger stability.

No Liberian court has tried anyone for the massacre, according to the lawyers and newspapers covering the case. At the launch of a family foundation in Nimba County, reported in January 2023, Isaac Karto Jr., whose parents were killed in the massacre, called on President George Weah's government to support a war and economic crimes court. The people who killed his parents, he said, were remorseless while their victims lived in grief.

With no route to a court at home, four survivors turned to the United States. On 12 February 2018 the Center for Justice and Accountability and the law firm Debevoise & Plimpton filed a civil suit in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania against Moses Thomas, after an investigation carried out with the Monrovia-based Global Justice and Research Project. He had lived in the Philadelphia area since around 2000. The plaintiffs used pseudonyms, Jane W and John X, Y and Z, because of the risk of reprisals in Liberia. Three of the four described relatives killed in the attack.

The suit relied on two US laws that let foreign victims sue in US courts, the Alien Tort Statute and the Torture Victim Protection Act. It accused Thomas, who had led the army's Special Anti-Terrorist Unit, of extrajudicial killing, torture, war crimes and crimes against humanity. According to the Inquirer, the plaintiffs did not accuse him of killing anyone personally; the case was that he led the attack. Thomas moved to dismiss in April 2018, arguing that the time limit had passed and that the plaintiffs had not tried to use remedies in Liberia. The court rejected those arguments, finding in the account of The New Dawn that victims could not have sued in Liberia because no one had been tried there and they feared reprisals.

In a 2018 interview with the Inquirer, Thomas said the plaintiffs had the wrong man and that he had been at the presidential palace that night. "It's all lies," he said. The Inquirer reports that he closed a West African restaurant he helped run in Philadelphia and went back to Liberia a year after the suit was filed, while the Center for Justice and Accountability gives 2019 as the year he left the United States.

On 16 March 2021 the plaintiffs' lawyers filed a motion for summary judgment backed by almost 2,000 pages of evidence from a seven-year investigation. It included eyewitness testimony, an expert report from a former deputy chief of mission at the US embassy in Monrovia, and declassified embassy and CIA cables. On 15 September 2021 Judge Petrese Tucker granted it. In a 51-page decision she found Thomas liable for torture, extrajudicial killing, attempted extrajudicial killing, war crimes, crimes against humanity and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. "He intentionally directed an attack on a building dedicated to religion, personally directed an attack on civilians and committed the crime against humanity of persecution," she wrote. The Center for Justice and Accountability called it the first decision to hold a member of the Armed Forces of Liberia to account for abuses in the First Liberian Civil War. A Liberian newspaper's headline called the outcome "guilty", but it was a civil judgment and the court did not convict anyone of a crime.

On 16 August 2022, Magistrate Judge Lynne Sitarski ordered Thomas to pay each of the four plaintiffs $6 million in compensatory and $15 million in punitive damages, $84 million in all. She wrote that although no award could repair what the victims suffered, a substantial one might deter future abusers. Reached by phone, Thomas dismissed the order as "stupidity". Because he is in Liberia, the Inquirer said it was unlikely the plaintiffs would ever collect.

On 4 October 2022 the Center for Justice and Accountability, the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa and Debevoise & Plimpton filed a case at the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice, the West African regional court. The plaintiffs are the Global Justice and Research Project and three siblings who lost about 16 relatives in the church. The suit is against the Republic of Liberia, for its failure to investigate and prosecute the massacre or to provide redress. Its lawyers described it as the first time a court would examine Liberia's failure to investigate violations in its two civil wars. No ruling in that case has been reported.

The lawyers' position is that the US judgment is not enough. Catherine Amirfar of Debevoise said Liberia has an obligation under international law to investigate and prosecute. Hassan Bility, who directs the Global Justice and Research Project, said that until there is accountability at home survivors and victims cannot live in peace. In 2021 Alain Werner, a lawyer in Geneva who has helped Liberian war victims bring cases, told the Inquirer that Thomas still wields influence at home, since many soldiers who served under him now hold fairly high positions in the security forces. The Inquirer noted reports alleging that Thomas had tried to identify and intimidate potential witnesses. Liberia has not announced any investigation of the massacre in the reporting available.
